section_title: Whom does God mark as His own before judgment falls?

versions.label: BSB
paragraphs: 1 After this I saw four angels standing at the four corners of the earth, holding back its four winds so that no wind would blow on land or sea or on any tree. 2 And I saw another angel ascending from the east, with the seal of the living God. And he called out in a loud voice to the four angels who had been given power to harm the land and the sea: 3 “Do not harm the land or sea or trees until we have placed a seal on the foreheads of the servants of our God.”

4 And I heard the number of those who were sealed, 144,000 from all the tribes of Israel: 5 From the tribe of Judah 12,000 were sealed, from the tribe of Reuben 12,000, from the tribe of Gad 12,000, 6 from the tribe of Asher 12,000, from the tribe of Naphtali 12,000, from the tribe of Manasseh 12,000, 7 from the tribe of Simeon 12,000, from the tribe of Levi 12,000, from the tribe of Issachar 12,000, 8 from the tribe of Zebulun 12,000, from the tribe of Joseph 12,000, and from the tribe of Benjamin 12,000.

context_lines: Before the seventh seal is opened, John sees a pause in the threatened harm. Four angels hold back the winds, and another angel comes from the east with the seal of the living God. The command is to wait until God’s servants have been sealed on their foreheads.

The scene answers the fear raised at the end of chapter 6 with attention to people who belong to God. The harm is restrained while His servants are identified. The description calls them His servants before speaking of their sealing.

John hears a number: 144,000, with 12,000 from each named tribe of Israel. Judah comes first. Levi and Joseph appear, while Dan and the name Ephraim do not. The passage gives the list without stating the reason for every inclusion or omission.

The number is followed by the vision of an uncountable multitude from every nation. How the two groups relate is a major question in interpretation. The text first lets us hear the numbered list and then see the multitude, and both scenes deserve to be read in their full setting.
common_interpretation_lines: Christian readings differ over the identity and number of those sealed. [Walvoord](https://swartzentrover.com/cotor/E-Books/holiness/Walvoord/Revelation/Rev_07.htm) reads 144,000 Israelites protected during a future tribulation. [Wesley](https://wesley.nnu.edu/john-wesley/john-wesleys-notes-on-the-bible/notes-on-the-revelation-of-jesus-christ/) also understands Israelites secured from coming calamities, while explaining that the number does not include every Israelite who will ever be saved. These readings take the tribal identification as referring to Israel’s people.

[Gill](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/revelation/7.htm) instead understands the number as representing God’s people across nations and ages. The [USCCB notes](https://bible.usccb.org/bible/revelation/7) likewise read it symbolically, as the new Israel embracing people from every nation. This is a genuine difference over how the tribal list functions in the vision, rather than a disagreement that can be resolved simply by assuming one meaning for every number in Revelation.

The identity of the angel bearing the seal is also interpreted differently. Gill identifies him with Christ acting for His people; Wesley understands a good angel carrying out God’s commission. The passage calls him an angel and describes his authority without giving a name. Both readings emphasize that the servants’ security comes from God.
god_plan_lines: The mark on the forehead recalls [Ezekiel 9:1–6](https://biblehub.com/bsb/ezekiel/9.htm), where those grieving over Jerusalem’s wrongdoing are marked before judgment. The parallel draws attention to God knowing His people amid the evil around them.

[Ephesians 1:13–14](https://biblehub.com/bsb/ephesians/1.htm) also uses sealing for believers’ relationship with God, identifying the Holy Spirit as the pledge of their inheritance. That does not make every detail of these passages identical, but it places Revelation’s scene within a wider biblical theme: those who belong to God are known to Him and held within His purpose. The following vision will show His people brought out of suffering into His presence.
